live_web_research.page_text: [2610.12310] Is In-Domain Training Enough for Fine-Grained Industrial Anomaly Understanding? Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition arXiv:2610.12310 (cs) [Submitted on 8 Oct 2026] Title: Is In-Domain Training Enough for Fine-Grained Industrial Anomaly Understanding? Authors: Xingwu Zhang , Duanyang Du , Huiling Zhu , Jiayue Dai , Yixiao Liu , Guozhi Liu , Zhihan Zhang , Zijun Long View a PDF of the paper titled Is In-Domain Training Enough for Fine-Grained Industrial Anomaly Understanding?, by Xingwu Zhang and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A single multimodal large language model (MLLM) struggles to excel simultaneously at detection, localization, description, and reasoning in multimodal industrial anomaly understanding (MM-IAU). We show that in-domain training does not close this gap. On MMAD, a widely adopted MM-IAU benchmark, trained specialists reach at most 75.5% accuracy in defect localization, against 92.3% for human experts, and even detect anomalies less accurately than their untrained base model. Meanwhile, different MLLMs offer complementary strengths but share this weakness in fine-grained perception, so combining them alone cannot remove it. We therefore propose SiGMA, a spatially grounded multi-agent framework that divides labor between heterogeneous MLLM agents and a dedicated visual defect expert. A multimodal searcher supplies industrial knowledge and normal references, the defect expert turns query-reference comparison into calibrated anomaly evidence, and a label-free reliability controller weighs each source by task-wise competence and query-level evidence quality. SiGMA reaches 85.2% average accuracy on MMAD, 4.0% above the strongest trained specialist and Gemini-2.5-Pro and within 1.5% of human experts. Even with three agents of at most 9B parameters, it reaches 84.4%, and new MLLMs join without retraining. live_web_research.snippet: Mar 13, 2026 · Why manufacturing is the proving ground for physical AI Manufacturing is uniquely positioned at the center of this shift. AI is no longer confined to planning or analytics.
live_web_research.page_text: Why physical AI is becoming manufacturing’s next advantage | MIT Technology Review Skip to Content Sponsored Provided by Microsoft and NVIDIA For decades, manufacturers have pursued automation to drive efficiency, reduce costs, and stabilize operations. That approach delivered meaningful gains, but it is no longer enough. Today’s manufacturing leaders face a different challenge: how to grow amid labor constraints, rising complexity, and increasing pressure to innovate faster without sacrificing safety, quality, or trust. The next phase of transformation will not be defined by isolated AI tools or individual robots, but by intelligence that can operate reliably in the physical world . This is where physical AI—intelligence that can sense, reason, and act in the real world—marks a decisive shift. And it is why Microsoft and NVIDIA are working together to help manufacturers move from experimentation to production at industrial scale. The industrial frontier: Intelligence and trust, not just automation Most early AI adoption focused on narrow optimization: automating tasks, improving utilization, and cutting costs. While valuable, that phase often created new friction, including skills gaps, governance concerns, and uncertainty about long‑term impact. Furthermore, the use cases were plentiful but not as strategic. The industrial frontier represents a different approach. Rather than asking how much work machines can replace, frontier manufacturers ask how AI can expand human capability, accelerate innovation, and unlock new forms of value while remaining trustworthy and controllable. Across industries, companies that successfully move into this frontier phase share two non‑negotiables: Intelligence: AI systems must understand how the business actually handles its data, workflows, and institutional knowledge. Trust: As AI begins to act in high‑stakes environments, organizations must retain security, governance, and observability at every layer. Without intelligence, AI becomes generic. Without trust, adoption stalls. Why manufacturing is the proving ground for physical AI Manufacturing is uniquely positioned at the center of this shift. AI is no longer confined to planning or analytics. It is moving into physical execution: coordinating machines, adapting to real‑world variability, and working alongside people on the factory floor. Robotics, autonomous systems, and AI agents must now perceive, reason, and act in dynamic environments. This transition exposes a critical gap. Traditional automation excels at repetition but struggles with adaptability. Human workers bring judgment and context but are constrained by scale. Physical AI closes that gap by enabling human‑led, AI‑operated systems, where people set intent and intelligent systems execute, learn, and improve over time. Humans are essential for scaled success. Microsoft and NVIDIA: Accelerating physical AI at scale Physical AI cannot be delivered through point solutions. It requires agentic-driven, enterprise-grade development, deployment, and operations toolchains and workflows that connect simulation, data, AI models, robotics, and governance into a coherent system. NVIDIA is building the AI infrastructure that makes physical AI possible, including accelerated computing, open models, simulation libraries, and robotics frameworks and blueprints that enable the ecosystem to build autonomous robotics systems that can perceive, reason, plan, and take action in the physical world. Microsoft complements this with a cloud and data platform designed to operate physical AI securely, at scale, and across the enterprise . Together, Microsoft and NVIDIA are enabling manufacturers to move beyond pilots toward production‑ready physical AI systems that can be developed, tested, deployed, and continuously improved across heterogeneous environments spanning the product lifecycle, factory operations, and supply chain. From intelligence to action: Human-agent teams in the factory At the industrial frontier, AI is not a standalone system, but a digital teammate. When AI agents are grounded in the proper operational data, embedded in human workflows, and governed end to end, they can assist with tasks such as: Optimizing production lines in real time Coordinating maintenance and quality decisions Adapting operations to supply or demand disruptions Accelerating engineering and product lifecycle decisions For example, manufacturers are beginning to use simulation‑grounded AI agents to evaluate production changes virtually before deploying them on the factory floor, reducing risk while accelerating decision‑making. Crucially, frontier manufacturers design these systems so humans remain in control. AI executes, monitors, and recommends, while people provide intent, oversight, and judgment. This balance allows organizations to move faster without losing confidence or control. The role of trust in scaling physical AI As physical AI systems scale, trust becomes the limiting factor. Manufacturers must ensure that AI systems are secure, observable, and operating within policy, especially when they influence safety‑critical or mission‑critical processes. Governance cannot be an afterthought; It must be engineered into the platform itself. This is why frontier manufacturers treat trust as a first‑class requirement, pairing innovation with visibility, compliance, and accountability. Only then can physical AI move from promising demonstrations to enterprise‑wide deployment. Why this moment matters—and what’s next The convergence of AI agents, robotics, simulation, and real‑time data marks an inflection point for manufacturing. What was once experimental is becoming operational. What was once siloed is becoming connected. At NVIDIA GTC 2026 , Microsoft and NVIDIA will demonstrate how this collaboration supports physical AI systems that manufacturers can deploy today and scale responsibly tomorrow. From simulation‑driven development to real‑world execution, the focus is on helping manufacturers cross the industrial frontier with confidence. For manufacturing leaders, the question is no longer whether physical AI will reshape operations, but how quickly they can adopt it responsibly, at scale, and with trust built in from the start. live_web_research.page_text: AI Agents in Manufacturing: 2026 Report | Customertimes Services Products Insights Company Contact us What are AI agents in manufacturing? AI agents in manufacturing are autonomous software systems that monitor plant and business data, reason about what they observe, and take actions creating maintenance work orders when vibration signatures degrade, triaging quality defects, rebalancing supply plans when a supplier slips, or resolving warranty cases. They differ from the industrial copilots most manufacturers piloted in 2024, 2025: a copilot answers when asked; an agent acts on triggers and schedules, escalating to humans only when confidence is low or an approval threshold is crossed. The distinction matters because the economics differ. A copilot saves minutes per query. An agent removes an entire monitoring-and-response loop from human queues. That is why 2026's dominant industrial AI project is not deploying new copilots, it is upgrading 2025's copilot deployments to agentic execution. 15–30% Unplanned downtime reduction from predictive maintenance agents 30–50% Autonomous resolution for service & warranty case agents 80% Of manufacturing AI pilots stall before production – the problem agents inherit if data isn't ready The six production-ready agent use cases in 2026 Agent use case What it does autonomously 2026 status Measured impact 1. Predictive maintenance agent Converts anomaly detection into scheduled work orders, parts orders, and technician dispatch Production at scale 15–30% downtime reduction; ~95% of deployments ROI-positive; 27% reach 12-month payback 2. Quality triage agent Pairs computer-vision detection (98–99% accuracy) with defect disposition, root-cause categorization, and containment initiation Production at scale 40–60% manual inspection labor reduction 3. Supply chain rebalancing agent Detects supplier slips and demand shifts; proposes or executes plan changes within approval limits Production (approval-gated) Days-to-hours replanning cycles 4. Service & warranty case agent Resolves dealer/customer cases end-to-end from knowledge and entitlement data; escalates exceptions Production at scale 30–50% autonomous resolution; 20–35% faster first response 5. Sales & CPQ agent Configures, prices, and quotes complex product lines; drafts proposals grounded in ERP availability Production (complex-product niches) Quote cycles cut from days to hours 6. Frontline knowledge agent Turns manuals, SOPs, and tribal knowledge into guided, step-aware procedures for operators and technicians Production at scale Faster onboarding; measurable first-time-fix improvement Not yet production-ready: fully autonomous production scheduling and closed-loop process control on safety-rated systems remain pilot-stage, treat vendor claims there with scrutiny. Agentforce, industrial platforms, or custom builds? The platform decision follows the action surface, where the agent reads and writes: If the agent acts on… Best-fit platform Why Customer-facing & business processes: service, warranty, dealer management, sales/CPQ Salesforce Agentforce CRM data grounding, guardrails, audit trails, and escalation built in; consumption pricing; fastest time-to-production. See our Agentforce for discrete manufacturing analysis. OT / shop-floor systems in real time: historians, MES, SCADA Industrial stacks (Siemens Industrial Copilot, NVIDIA-accelerated platforms) or custom Latency, protocol, and safety-rating requirements CRM platforms don't address Both (most manufacturers) Hybrid, connected via a unified data layer (Salesforce Data Cloud, Databricks) The integration architecture — not the agent framework — is where programs succeed or fail. See our manufacturing data activation blueprint . The 90-day implementation path Weeks 1–2: Data readiness assessment. Inventory the systems the agent must read/write; measure master-data duplicate rates (target <5% on assets, parts, customers); audit knowledge content currency. Weeks 3–6: Grounding and integration. Connect ERP/CRM/MES sources through governed APIs; build the agent's write-path (work orders, cases, plan changes), the step 80% of stalled pilots never designed. Weeks 7–9: Configuration and guardrail testing. Define topics, actions, approval thresholds; adversarial testing against historical cases. AI-accelerated test harnesses (Customertimes uses Claude-based automation) compress this phase 40–50%. Weeks 10–13: Phased rollout. Launch on a slice (one line, one product family, one dealer region); monitor resolution and escalation accuracy; expand on evidence. Full methodology, cost benchmarks, and partner-evaluation criteria: our Agentforce implementation guide and the AI Automation in Manufacturing report , which covers the full six-category vendor landscape (71 vendors) this agent layer builds on. Frequently asked questions Want to apply but still have questions? Explore our FAQ for detailed answers. What is the difference between an industrial copilot and an AI agent? A copilot answers when a human asks. An agent watches the data and acts on its own, opening the work order, ordering the part, notifying the planner, escalating only on low confidence or set approval thresholds. Copilot adoption grew fast through 2025; 2026 is the upgrade cycle into agents. What ROI should we expect, honestly? On unified, ready data: meaningful gains in downtime reduction (predictive maintenance), inspection labor (quality triage), and autonomous case resolution (service/warranty). On disconnected ERP, CRM, and MES data: underperformance across the board. Data readiness is the ROI variable, not the platform. Why do most manufacturing AI pilots stall before production? Pilots get built on extracted data samples, with no write-path for actions, no change management for affected roles, and no owner for post-launch tuning. Agents make that worse if left unaddressed, and dramatically better when the pilot runs on live, integrated data with a designed action path. What data infrastructure is the minimum? Unified access to the systems the agent touches, low duplicate rates in master data, a grounding layer built from manuals and SOPs, governed APIs for taking action, and audit logging on every autonomous step. How do we choose an implementation partner for agentic AI? Demand production references with real numbers (resolution rates, rollback history), a partner that combines data and integration capability on one team rather than siloed specialists, and senior-heavy staffing for the architecture work. selected_records.title: Is In-Domain Training Enough for Fine-Grained Industrial Anomaly Understanding?

article.body:
Industrial anomaly paper reports benchmark gains, not factory deployment

A new arXiv paper proposes SiGMA, a framework combining multimodal language-model agents with a visual defect expert to detect and localize industrial anomalies. On the MMAD benchmark, trained specialists reached at most 75.5% accuracy in defect localization, versus 92.3% for human experts. SiGMA scored 85.2% average accuracy; a three-agent version using models of at most 9 billion parameters scored 84.4%.

The work reports benchmark results, not operation on a production line. It specifies no factory, inspection throughput, production capacity or deployment. The documented constraint is fine-grained perception: in-domain training did not close the localization gap. No customer, supplier or supply-chain effect is established.
